# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–8 (Complete and Final – Updated 82)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; nearly three weeks into new year (1832) after Lords threw out Reform Bill; summer and autumn of first year; winter of first year; Vauxhall evening during spring of first year; spring of second year; summer of second year; autumn of second year; winter of second year; narrative extends into future years; present day with Fred and Mary at Stone Court in white-haired placidity
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring, Wilhaven, Salford, Chiswick Mall, Hammersmith, Soho, Thames, England, Oxford, Chiswick Church, Buxton, Kensington turnpike, Russell Square, London, Southampton Row, Vauxhall, Exeter 'Change, India (Boggley Wollah, Ramgunge, Budgebudge, Calcutta, Dumdum), Forty Thieves theatre, King's 14th regiment post, Highbury Barn, Covent Garden Market, Doctor Swishtail's Seminary, Bedford tavern, Thames Street (City), Royal Gardens, St. George's Hanover Square, Lambeth Palace, Great Gaunt Street, Queen's Crawley (Hants), Mudbury, Gaunt Square, Mansion House, Oxford Street, Swallow Street, Cambridge, Leakington, Squashmore, Bethesda Chapel Liverpool, Naples, Paris, Eton, Pumpernickel, Strasburg, Crawley parish, Yarlton, Quashimaboo, Fuddleston, Roxby, Wapshot Hall, Christchurch, Rectory House, Hampshire, Chiswick, Coldcombe, Huddleston, Cocoa-Tree, Woolwich, hill farms of Coldcombe, Humdrum Hall, Wattier's, Chatham, Horse Guards, Carlton House, St. Kitt's, Opera, Prince Regent locations, Demerara, St. Vincent's, Quebec, Charing Cross, Pall Mall, Old Slaughters', West Indies, Rochester, Chatham barracks, hill farms of Fenmere, Knightsbridge Barracks, Park Lane, Hants, Life Guards, 150th regiment depot at Mudbury, Dunholt village, Bloomsbury, Russell Square, Harrowgate, Great Gaunt Street (hatchment location), hill farms of Mirecombe, harbor town of Wilhaven
- **Narrative Presence**: Narrator warns Vanity Fair is "a very vain, wicked, foolish place, full of all sorts of humbugs and falsenesses and pretensions"; observes human hearts and self-deceptions with ironic sympathy; reflects on marriage bargains mothers and daughters make daily

## Main Characters

**Rebecca Sharp (Miss Becky)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Age nineteen; father artist/drawing teacher at Miss Pinkerton's academy; mother French opera-girl
- Small, slight, pale, sandy-haired with large attractive eyes; white slender fingers
- Skilled musician, linguist, artist; speaks French with purity; proficient in globes
- Determined, observant, capable of calculated charm; speaks with slight foreign accent when agitated
- **Current Role**: Companion and nurse to Miss Crawley at Park Lane residence; indispensable; controls household and sickroom access; maintains composed appearance; never out of temper; nerves of iron
- **Social Manipulations**: Received new gowns, necklace, shawl from Miss Crawley; shows Miss Crawley the affection of an intimate companion; has been made acquainted with George's opinions of her (sharp, dangerous, dangerous flirt) within twenty-four hours of his confiding them to Rawdon; woman's instinct told her George interrupted her first love-passage with Rawdon; esteems him accordingly; uses this knowledge strategically
- **Encounter with George Osborne**: Greeted him with studied coolness when he visited—gave little finger with cool, killing nod when he extended left hand patronizingly; devastated his confidence; responded with self-deprecating but shrewd remarks about her position as governess in gentleman's family; referenced Sir Pitt's father refusing peerage; deflected his condescension; made him jealous by praising Amelia; asked pointedly about Joseph Sedley; had clearly won the exchange—George could not take revenge, only confide his suspicions to Rawdon
- **Miss Crawley's Attachment**: Miss Crawley will not hear of her departure despite Sir Pitt's urgent entreaties; as long as Miss Crawley's engagement lasts, her attachment is prodigious; clings with greatest energy to Rebecca
- **Gravest Upon Lady Crawley's Death**: When news of Lady Crawley's death came, Rebecca seemed by far gravest and most impressed of family; left room before Rawdon; met him by chance below for parley

**Captain Rawdon Crawley** [CHARACTER]
- Captain in Life Guards; celebrated "blood" or dandy; expert boxer, rat-hunter, four-in-hand driver; very large, six feet high; generous; over head and ears in debt; known gambler, drunkard, profligate
- Miss Crawley almost adopted him; designated for fifty thousand pounds in will
- **Love for Rebecca**: Completely victimized; barbed shaft of love penetrated his dull hide; raves about her; during romantic campaign faced perpetual defeats; perpetually routed; recognized Mrs. Bute's matchmaking scheme
- **Recent Activity**: Won two hundred pounds from George Osborne at billiards at Cocoa-Tree; invited Osborne to dinners at Miss Crawley's; praised Osborne's horsemanship; introduced him to fashionable young men; watched Rebecca's coolness to Osborne from other room and could hardly restrain laughter at his discomfiture; confided George's suspicions about Rebecca next day; laughed in agreement with George's assessments; heard Rebecca's name and opinions before twenty-four hours passed
- **Upon Lady Crawley's Death**: Remarked "What a confounded rage Pitt will be in if he does" (marry again) with usual regard for elder brother; after leaving Miss Crawley's, grasped crape hat and addressed Rebecca: "Come as Lady Crawley, if you like...Come back and be my wife. Your vit vor't. Birth be hanged. You're as good a lady as ever I see...Will you come? Yes or no?"—explicit marriage proposal to Rebecca

**Miss Crawley** [CHARACTER]
- Inherited large fortune; silly, romantic; very attached to Rawdon; adores imprudent matches
- Captivated by Amelia through Rebecca's introduction; praised her complexion and voice; visited Russell Square
- **Current Relationship with Rebecca**: Quite overcome by little governess; orders Rebecca sit at dinners; demands her presence; gave new gowns, necklace, shawl; shows friendship by abusing intimate acquaintances; good taste for natural manners and pretty faces
- **Response to Lady Crawley's Death**: "I suppose I must put off my party for the 3rd"; added after pause, "I hope my brother will have the decency not to marry again"; will not hear of Rebecca's departure; as long as engagement lasts, attachment prodigious; clings with greatest energy to Rebecca

**George Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Handsome; jolly, sociable; excellent at games, billiards, field-sports, song, parade; adored by men; famous drinker and sparrer
- Over head and ears in debt; known gambler, drunkster, profligate; shot Captain Marker in duel; robbed young Lord Dovedale
- **Engagement to Amelia**: Engaged; furious upon learning regiment knows; admits "I am very fond of Amelia; I adore her"; acknowledges "She's faultless"; took tender leave of Amelia
- **Financial Transaction**: Visited City; received document from Mr. Chopper; exchanged at Hulker & Bullock's for pocketful of money; was "much too elated"
- **Gambling and Visits**: Won two hundred pounds from Rawdon at billiards at Cocoa-Tree; would have played for anything that day before Dobbin intervention; described as "young flat" by Rawdon; Rawdon invited him to dinners; praised his horsemanship; introduced him to fashionable young men; visit immensely elated simple young officer
- **Encounter with Rebecca**: Approached her with patronizing, easy swagger; intended to be kind and protect her; held out left hand expecting she would be confounded at honor; she put out right forefinger with cool, killing nod that devastated his confidence; her response to his condescension was self-deprecating but strategically superior—she deflected his patronage with remarks about her gentleman's family status and referenced Sir Pitt's refused peerage; made him jealous about Amelia; asked about Joseph Sedley; had clearly won exchange
- **Confiding to Rawdon**: Unable to take revenge on Rebecca, confided to Rawdon next day that she was "a sharp one, a dangerous one, a desperate flirt"; Rawdon agreed laughingly; Rebecca was made acquainted with these opinions within twenty-four hours; opinions added to her original regard for Osborne; her woman's instinct had identified him as interrupter of her first love-passage with Rawdon

**Amelia Sedley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Rebecca's former schoolfriend; small, modest, unaffected; tender heart; timid; sweet modest soul
- **Relationship with George**: Confirmed engagement; believes deeply in George; innocent and trusting; assumes his errands legitimate; loves him completely
- **Actual Behavior**: Leaves home daily; dines abroad six days week; neglected twelve Chiswick friends; made confidante of Laura Martin; promised Laura would live with her when married
- **Letters to George**: Extraordinarily long and passionate; filled large paper sheets crossed with perverseness; whole pages of poetry; underlined words with frantic emphasis; repetitive; doubtful grammar; numerous notes followed him
- **Recent**: Visited briefly with Rebecca when Miss Crawley called on Russell Square; came down with kind smiling looks; blushed kissing Rebecca; impressed Miss Crawley with "sweet blushing face"
- **Worries**: Unaware of George's financial transaction; worries her poor papa melancholy; sent George tenderest letter with foreboding evil

**Lady Crawley (formerly Rose Dawson)** [CHARACTER – DECEASED]
- Sir Pitt's wife; otherwise friendless; sold her heart to become Sir Pitt Crawley's wife; heart dead long before body; had known only Sir Pitt's kindness and Mr. Crawley's friendship
- **Death**: Died during winter of second year while Sir Pitt attended to schemes in London; hatchment placed over Sir Pitt's house in Great Gaunt Street—feminine hatchment, formerly used for Sir Pitt's old mother (late dowager Lady Crawley); arms not hers (she had no arms), but cherubs and Resurgam served; arms quartered with Crawley Dove and Serpent
- **Final Years**: Mr. Crawley tended her bedside; she went out of world strengthened by his words and comfort; his was only kindness she ever knew; feeble, lonely soul
- **Death Location**: Harbor town of Wilhaven
- **Significance**: Her death presents opportunity for Sir Pitt to remarry; her marriage exemplifies bargain mothers and daughters make daily in Vanity Fair

**Other Characters**
- **Old Mr. Osborne**: Wealthy merchant; ordered George to collect money from Chopper; stated Sedley's affairs look bad
- **Sir Pitt Crawley**: Old, stumpy, short, vulgar; widower now; sent nearly daily franks to Rebecca with urgent prayers for her return; despaired at her absence while wife was ill; called often in Park Lane; despached many notes to Rebecca entreating, enjoining, commanding her to return to pupils
- **Mr. Pitt Crawley** (son): Expected to be in a "confounded rage" if Sir Pitt remarries; Rawdon regards his prospective anger with usual brotherly carelessness
- **Captain Dobbin**: Carried off George Osborne from billiards
- **Old John Sedley**: Observed leaving banker's parlour looking dismal
- **Laura Martin**: Amelia's confidante; promised to live with Amelia when married
- **Mrs. Bute Crawley**: Made confidante by Rawdon; warned him appropriately
- **Miss Briggs**: Displaced by Rebecca; position now sinecure and derision
- **Rose and Violet Crawley**: Young pupils left without companionship during mother's illness; pupils Sir Pitt wants Rebecca to return to

## Critical Facts and Status
- Rebecca indispensable to Miss Crawley; Miss Crawley will not release her despite Sir Pitt's desperate entreaties
- Rawdon has explicitly proposed marriage to Rebecca following Lady Crawley's death
- Rebecca's response to Rawdon's proposal not yet recorded
- Lady Crawley dead; Sir Pitt now widower; Sir Pitt hopes not to remarry
- Rebecca strategically defeated George Osborne in their encounter; gained intelligence of his suspicions; positioned herself as superior
- George's financial gains coincide with Sedley family troubles; timing suggests crisis
- Amelia innocent of these developments; trusts George completely; worries about family
- Woman's instinct identified George as interrupter of Rebecca's first romantic passage with Rawdon; Rebecca esteems him accordingly—likely means she respects his judgment while remaining strategically aware
- Sir Pitt's letters show spelling and tenor of his desperate distress at Rebecca's absence
- Marriage presented as daily bargain in Vanity Fair; Lady Crawley's death exemplifies this
